title: Hot inflation, a CEO exit and a 5% yield: the week stocks rose anyway

questions.q: On Thursday the 2-year Treasury yield rose 13 basis points and the 10-year rose 12, and Reuters said short-term yields had risen more than long-term ones for a fourth straight session. What is that pattern called, and what does it signal?
options: A Treasury auction tail; it signals that the government has stopped borrowing
A relief rally; it signals that bond prices are recovering
A flattening yield curve; it signals that investors expect the Fed to push short-term rates up now
A risk premium; it signals that oil supply is in danger
questions.explain: The {{yield-curve|yield curve}} flattens when short-term yields rise faster than long-term ones. The {{two-year-yield|2-year yield}} follows the Fed's next few moves most closely, so it led the way in a week when traders priced in a December {{rate-hike|rate hike}}.

questions.q: On Thursday President Trump posted that a deal with Iran was no longer needed, and WTI crude rose about 2.6% to $88.74. No oil supply was actually lost that day. What explains the jump?
options: The risk premium for the Strait of Hormuz went back into the price once hopes for a deal faded
US crude inventories fell to zero
The Fed cut interest rates
A stronger dollar always makes oil more expensive in dollars
questions.explain: A {{risk-premium|risk premium}} is the extra amount buyers pay because something might go wrong. Hopes for a US–Iran deal had been holding {{wti|WTI}} down; when the hope was removed, the price rose even though supply had not changed.

questions.q: CoreWeave lost $709 million in the quarter, yet its stock rose about 24% on Wednesday. One reason was that its revenue backlog reached about $132.5 billion, up from $104 billion in June. What does that number tell investors?
options: How much cash the company has in the bank
How much the company owes its lenders
How many shares were traded after hours
How much future revenue is already under signed contract but not yet delivered
questions.explain: A {{revenue-backlog|revenue backlog}} is work customers have already agreed to pay for. Investors had been asking whether AI spending could last, and a growing backlog, together with raised {{earnings-guidance|guidance}}, answered that worry for the moment.

questions.q: On Thursday a sale of new 30-year Treasury bonds “tailed” by half a basis point. What does that mean?
options: The sale was cancelled for lack of bidders
The government had to pay a slightly higher yield than the market expected, a sign of lackluster demand
The bonds were sold only to small investors
The bonds' yield came out lower than expected because demand was strong
questions.explain: In a {{treasury-auction|Treasury auction}} the government sells debt to the highest bidders. A tail means buyers demanded more yield than expected. It came on a day when the 10-year {{treasury-yield|Treasury yield}} was already jumping to 5.10%.

questions.q: Tuesday's CPI came in above forecasts and Friday's PPI came in below them, yet both reports worried the bond market. What did the two reports have in common?
options: Both showed prices falling across the board
In both, energy had stopped driving prices up while the rest of the basket kept rising
Both were delayed by the Veterans Day holiday
Both showed gasoline as the main source of inflation
questions.explain: In the {{cpi|CPI}}, energy slowed sharply but {{core-inflation|core}} prices still rose 0.3%. In the {{ppi|PPI}}, energy fell 0.1% while the measure without foods, energy and trade services rose 0.5%. Inflation that has spread beyond fuel does not fade when oil gets cheaper, which is why yields kept rising.

questions.q: On Wednesday the Nasdaq rose 1.6% while the bond market was closed, and the brief called Thursday “the real test.” What did Thursday show?
options: Bonds rallied and yields fell, confirming the stock rally
The bond market stayed closed for a second day
Stocks no longer react to interest rates
The rate pressure had only been switched off for a day: the 10-year yield jumped to 5.10% and small-cap stocks fell about 1.7%
questions.explain: With bonds closed, {{treasury-yield|Treasury yields}} could not rise on Wednesday. When trading resumed, the 10-year gained 12 {{basis-point|basis points}} from Tuesday, and {{small-cap|small-cap}} companies, which rely more on borrowing, were hit hardest.

questions.q: Monday's brief asked whether the chip-led rebound was a real turn or only a relief rally. By Friday the S&P 500 had gained 2.5% for the week and ended a four-week losing streak. What is the fairest reading?
options: The rebound survived a hot CPI report and a 10-year yield above 5%, but Friday's 2.0% drop in technology shows the pressure from rates has not gone away
It was only a relief rally, because stocks ended the week lower than they started
Interest rates stopped mattering to stocks after Monday
The rebound happened because Treasury yields fell all week
questions.explain: A {{relief-rally|relief rally}} fades when the original problem returns. This one held through the week's tests, helped by CoreWeave's results on Wednesday, which gave {{dip-buying|dip-buyers}} a reason. But yields ended the week higher, and on Friday technology fell while {{defensive-stocks|defensive stocks}} rose.

questions.q: Gold fell 2.6% on Tuesday and about 3% on Thursday. On both days Treasury yields and the dollar index rose. Why do those two moves push gold down?
options: Gold miners must pay the Fed's interest rate on their output
A stronger dollar means the US government sells its gold reserves
Gold pays no interest and is priced in dollars, so higher yields and a stronger dollar both make it less attractive to hold
Gold only falls when oil rises
questions.explain: When {{treasury-yield|Treasury yields}} rise, bonds pay more while gold still pays nothing. When the {{dollar-index|dollar index}} rises, gold costs more for buyers using other currencies. The link held from Tuesday to Thursday; Friday, when gold was about flat, was the exception the sources did not explain.
